content: Pneumococcal disease is a severe illness that causes significant morbidity and mortality. It is responsible for more deaths annually in the United States than all other vaccine-preventable diseases combined. While anyone can contract pneumococcal disease, certain groups are at higher risk. These include individuals aged 65 and older, young children, and those with specific health conditions such as alcoholism, heart or lung disease, kidney failure, diabetes, HIV infection, or certain cancers. Pneumococcal disease can result in serious infections, including pneumonia (lung infection), bacteremia (blood infection), and meningitis (infection of the brain's protective covering). Approximately 1 in 20 individuals with pneumococcal pneumonia, 2 in 10 with bacteremia, and 3 in 10 with meningitis succumb to the disease. Those with underlying health conditions are at an even greater risk of death. Although antibiotics like penicillin were once effective in treating pneumococcal infections, increasing resistance to these drugs has made treatment more challenging, underscoring the importance of prevention through vaccination. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV) provides protection against 23 types of pneumococcal bacteria. Most healthy adults who receive the vaccine develop immunity to most or all of these bacterial types within 2 to 3 weeks. However, the vaccine may be less effective in very elderly individuals, children under 2 years of age, and those with certain chronic illnesses. The vaccine is recommended for all adults aged 65 years and older. It is also advised for individuals over 2 years of age who have chronic health conditions such as heart disease, lung disease, sickle cell disease, diabetes, alcoholism, cirrhosis, or cerebrospinal fluid leaks. Additionally, it is recommended for those with conditions or diseases that compromise the immune system, such as Hodgkin's disease, lymphoma, leukemia, kidney failure, multiple myeloma, nephrotic syndrome, HIV/AIDS, or those with a damaged or absent spleen. Individuals undergoing treatments that suppress the immune system, such as long-term steroid use, certain cancer therapies, or radiation therapy, should also receive the vaccine. Furthermore, Alaskan Natives and certain Native American populations are advised to be vaccinated. Typically, a single dose of PPV is sufficient. However, a second dose may be necessary under specific circumstances. A second dose is recommended for individuals with a damaged or absent spleen, sickle cell disease, HIV/AIDS, cancer, leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, kidney failure, nephrotic syndrome, or those who have undergone an organ or bone marrow transplant. It is also recommended for individuals taking immunosuppressive medications, such as chemotherapy or long-term steroids. For children aged 10 years or younger, the second dose should be administered 3 years after the first dose, while those older than 10 years should receive it 5 years after the initial dose. Children who frequently experience ear infections, sinus infections, or other upper respiratory conditions but are otherwise healthy do not require the PPV vaccine for these conditions. While the vaccine may be less effective in individuals with weakened immune systems, it is still recommended for these individuals as they are at a higher risk of severe illness from pneumococcal disease. The safety of PPV during pregnancy has not been thoroughly studied. Although there is no evidence suggesting harm to the mother or fetus, pregnant women should consult their healthcare provider before receiving the vaccine. Women at high risk for pneumococcal disease are encouraged to be vaccinated prior to pregnancy, if possible. The PPV vaccine is considered very safe. Approximately half of those vaccinated may experience mild side effects, such as redness or pain at the injection site. Less than 1% of individuals may develop fever, muscle aches, or more severe local reactions. Severe allergic reactions are extremely rare. As with any medical intervention, there is a very small risk of serious complications, including death, but the risk of severe illness from the disease itself is far greater than the risks associated with the vaccine. In the event of a moderate or severe reaction, such as a severe allergic response (e.g., hives, difficulty breathing, or shock), immediate medical attention should be sought. Inform the healthcare provider of the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Healthcare providers are encouraged to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form for any adverse reactions. Individuals can also report reactions directly to VAERS by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting their website. In rare cases of serious vaccine-related injury, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) provides financial assistance for medical care. For more information, individuals can contact the program at 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For further information about the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, individuals are encouraged to consult their healthcare provider, contact their local or state health department's immunization program, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 or visiting the CDC's National Immunization Program website.
